title: The SQE four years on – facts and figures
pub: Solicitors Regulation Authority (research and publications), drawing on candidate data and Kaplan analyses
author: Solicitors Regulation Authority

dom.t: Solicitor entry: Diverse routes yield unequal attainment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source addresses SQE pass-rate disparities and neurodivergence analysis, not the cluster’s proposition about converting AI capability into reliable legal services through multidisciplinary implementation, substantive verification and task-specific evaluation. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position.

st.t: Solicitor entry: Diverse routes yield unequal attainment
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it reports broad ethnic and socio-economic participation alongside unequal attainment, treats the causes of disparities as complex and substantially unexplained, and identifies apprenticeships as the clearest encouraging route through their stronger outcomes and social-mobility profile.
qs: The overall solicitor apprentice pass rates have been around 71% for SQE1 and 93% for SQE2, compared with 66% and 85% for the whole cohort.

mo.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards
Research representation: Purposeful samples limit wider claims
Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Four-year qualification evidence, rather than AI-impact evidence
kp.d: The SRA report addresses solicitor qualification, candidate performance and training provision, without discussing AI. Its main dataset covers eight SQE1 and 12 SQE2 assessments between November 2021 and July 2025, involving more than 30,000 candidates assessed in 50 countries.
qs: The data is drawn from almost four years of SQE results. It covers eight SQE1 and 12 SQE2 assessments taken between November 2021 and July 2025, and more than 30,000 candidates assessed in 50 countries.

kp.k: Cumulative qualification outcomes differ from first-attempt sitting rates
kp.d: First-time sitting pass rates ranged from 46% to 60% for SQE1 and 69% to 84% for SQE2. Across all candidates, including multiple attempts, 19,281 (66%) had passed SQE1 and 10,718 (85%) SQE2. Among successful candidates, 82.1% passed SQE1 on their first attempt and 94.2% passed SQE2 on their first attempt; these are distinct denominators from sitting-level pass rates.
qs: The pass rates for candidates sitting SQE1 for the first time have ranged from 46% to 60%.
Of all candidates who have attempted SQE1 – including those who have had multiple attempts – 19,281 (66%) candidates have now passed.
The pass rates for candidates sitting SQE2 for the first time have ranged from 69% to 84%.
Of all candidates who have passed SQE1, 82.1% passed on their first attempt. The corresponding figure for SQE2 is 94.2%.

kp.k: Academic background explains some, not most, performance variation
kp.d: Kaplan's multivariate analysis associates university rank with 11.9% and degree classification with 10.6% of SQE1 score variance. SQE1 scores explain 23.5% of SQE2 score variance; SQE1 performance and university ranking together explain about 30%. Most variation remains unexplained by recorded characteristics. Motivation, aptitude and study time are proposed explanations, not measured findings.
qs: This multivariate analysis shows that the rank of the university attended by a candidate and their degree classification together explain about 22% of the variance in candidates' SQE1 scores - 11.9% for university rank and 10.6% for degree classification.
For SQE2 candidates, SQE1 performance and university ranking explain about 30% of the variance.
Most of the variance in candidates' scores cannot be explained by the data we have on their characteristics or backgrounds, either alone or in combination.
It is likely to be explained by factors we cannot measure such as motivation, aptitude, study time.

kp.k: Ethnic diversity coexists with persistent assessment disparities
kp.d: The report describes the internationally drawn SQE cohort as more ethnically diverse than the UK population and solicitor profession. Its November 2021–January 2025 table reports 28.4% Asian/Asian British, 6.6% Black/Black British and 47% White candidates. White candidates generally perform better in both assessments. Kaplan associates ethnicity alone with 7.6% of SQE1 and 4.2% of SQE2 score variance; the SRA stresses complex explanations and cites commissioned Exeter research rather than attributing the pass-rate gap solely to ethnicity.
qs: The SQE entry cohort, which includes candidates living in the UK and in other countries, is more ethnically diverse than the UK population, when compared with the 2021 census data.
White candidates have generally performed better than candidates of all other ethnicities, in both SQE1 and SQE2
Generally, a candidate's ethnic group alone explains 7.6% of the variance in SQE1 scores.
Ethnicity alone appears to account for 4.2% of the variance in candidates' SQE2 scores.

kp.k: Socioeconomic associations shrink when other factors are considered
kp.d: The SRA reports candidates across socioeconomic backgrounds, with around 37% from less privileged backgrounds. Descriptive results show lower-background candidates generally performing less well, but Kaplan's multivariate analysis attributes little SQE1 score variance independently to parents' education (0.3%) or household earner's occupation (0.1%). Background classification uses parental university attendance, household occupation around age 14 and secondary-school type.
qs: Around 37% of candidates are from less privileged backgrounds.
candidates from lower socio-economic backgrounds generally performed less well than candidates from higher socio-economic backgrounds

When other factors are taken into account, candidates' socio-economic background alone accounts for very little of the variance seen in SQE1 scores - 0.3% for parents' education and 0.1% for household earner's occupation.

kp.k: Women predominate, with assessment-specific differences in outcomes
kp.d: Among 31,582 candidates issued SQE1 and/or SQE2 results, 63% were female, 35% male and 2% selected other or preferred not to disclose. Cumulative SQE1 pass rates were 64% for women and 68% for men; the pattern reversed for SQE2, at 86% and 83% respectively.
qs: Of the 31,582 candidates to whom SQE1 and/or SQE2 results have been issued, 63% were female, 35% male and 2% selected the 'prefer not to say' or 'other' option.
64% of female and 68% of male candidates who have taken SQE1 have passed. For SQE2, 86% of female and 83% of male candidates who have taken the assessment have passed.

kp.k: Adjusted neurodivergent candidates performed slightly better
kp.d: Candidates disclosing disabilities generally performed at least as well as others, unlike the LPC pattern reported by the SRA. Kaplan's separate September 2024–July 2025 analysis concerned first-time candidates with reasonable adjustments for disclosed neurodivergent conditions, representing 5.6% of candidates assessed during that period. They achieved slightly higher scores and pass rates. The SRA presents this as reassurance about disadvantage, but the described evidence concerns this adjusted, disclosed subgroup.
qs: The data also shows that candidates who declare a disability perform at least as well as other candidates on the SQE.
It has looked at the data for candidates attempting the assessments for the first time who had a reasonable adjustment for a disclosed neurodivergent condition.
Across the sittings, 5.6% of candidates assessed in this period had a reasonable adjustment plan for a neurodivergent condition.
Overall, these candidates achieved slightly higher scores and pass rates than other candidates, providing assurance that neurodivergent candidates are not disadvantaged in the assessment.

kp.k: Apprenticeships combine workplace learning with strong assessment outcomes
kp.d: English solicitor apprentices work four days weekly and study on the fifth, and must pass both SQE assessments. The summary reports overall apprentice pass rates around 71% for SQE1 and 93% for SQE2, against 66% and 85% across the cohort. Apprentices are more likely to come from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, be White and be female. The report finds little performance difference between graduate and non-graduate apprentices and presents apprenticeships as supporting social mobility.
qs: Solicitor apprentices work for four days a week in legal practice and study on the fifth day.
The overall solicitor apprentice pass rates have been around 71% for SQE1 and 93% for SQE2, compared with 66% and 85% for the whole cohort.
It also shows there is little difference in the SQE performance between graduate and non-graduate apprentices.
solicitor apprenticeships in England are supporting social mobility, and solicitor apprentices are performing particularly well in their assessments with higher pass rates than the overall cohort

kp.k: Apprenticeship duration varies; funding eligibility narrowed in 2026
kp.d: School-leaver apprenticeships typically take six years, approximately the duration of university followed by SQE qualification; graduate apprenticeships typically take two to three years. The report states that a January 2026 government-policy change mainly limits apprentice funding to people aged 21 or under at commencement.
qs: A school leaver will typically take six years to complete their apprenticeship and qualify as a solicitor.
It is typically completed in two to three years.
A change in government policy took effect in January 2026. This means that funding for apprentices is mainly limited to those aged 21 or under when they start their apprenticeship.

kp.k: Cohort composition helps explain fluctuating sitting pass rates
kp.d: Resitters generally have lower pass rates, with around 20% passing SQE1 according to the summary. July 2025 had the highest resitter proportion and lowest SQE1 pass rate to date. Qualified lawyers also generally have lower pass rates: in October 2023 they constituted 34% of SQE2 candidates, with a 49% pass rate against 80% for other candidates and 64% overall. The SRA treats changing cohort composition as a partial explanation, not a complete account.
qs: Typically, around 20% of those who resit SQE1 pass.
The July 2025 SQE1 sitting had the highest proportion of re-sitting candidates seen to date. It also had the lowest pass rate.
In that sitting, 34% of candidates were qualified lawyers, the highest of any SQE2 sitting.
However, the pass rate for candidates who were not qualified lawyers was 80%; the pass rate for qualified lawyers was 49%.

kp.k: International assessment availability broadens qualification access
kp.d: The SQE replaced the Qualified Lawyers Transfer Scheme as the admission route for qualified lawyers. Written SQE1 and SQE2 assessments have been taken in 50 countries, while SQE2 oral assessments are restricted to England and Wales. The report says this improves accessibility for some, while documenting lower outcomes among qualified lawyers and non-native English speakers. For 2023/2024 sittings, English-first-language pass rates were 56% for SQE1 and 81% for SQE2, compared with 47% and 63% for other first languages.
qs: The opportunity to take the written SQE assessments in test centres across the world makes qualification as a solicitor in England and Wales more accessible for some.
The SQE2 oral assessments can only be taken in England and Wales.
Qualified lawyers and candidates whose first language is not English have generally had lower pass rates than the wider cohort.

kp.k: LPC graduates gain an alternative but demanding qualification route
kp.d: LPC graduates unable to secure recognised training can qualify through SQE2 plus two years' qualifying work experience; around 900 had successfully used this route. Their SQE2 pass rates are generally lower. The SRA explains that the LPC assesses readiness to start a training contract, whereas the SQE assesses readiness to practise, and advises preparation accordingly. Its accompanying table compares candidates with and without SQE1, rather than explicitly identifying every non-SQE1 candidate as an LPC graduate.
qs: Instead, they can now pass SQE2 and undertake two years' qualifying work experience. So far, around 900 LPC graduates have successfully taken this route to qualification.
The LPC was designed to assess individuals' readiness to start a training contract.
The SQE, in contrast, is designed to assess individuals' readiness to start practising as a solicitor – in other words, the SQE is, by its nature more demanding than the LPC.
We have reminded LPC graduates that they need to understand the SQE is more demanding than the LPC and prepare accordingly.

kp.k: Consistent standards are distinguished from speculative sponsorship effects
kp.d: The SRA says common-question analysis showed July 2025's SQE1 cohort was weaker than previous cohorts, including July 2024, and that resitter composition alone did not explain its lower pass rate. It maintains that standards are constant across sittings. Its suggestion that larger firms' January examination requirements partly explain January–July differences is explicitly speculative because sponsorship data are not collected.
qs: The analysis of the performance on the common questions in the July 2025 assessment showed that the July 2025 cohort was weaker than previous cohorts, including the July 2024 cohort.
We can only speculate as to why the July 2025 SQE1 cohort was weaker – and why recent July cohorts have been weaker than the January cohorts of the same year.
We do not collect data on whether candidates are sponsored, but we know that many of the larger law firms that sponsor candidates to take the SQE require them to take SQE1 in January.
the same standard is applied for all sittings and all candidates, regardless of where or when they are assessed.

kp.k: Training choices expand without SRA regulation of providers
kp.d: The SRA neither prescribes preparation nor regulates SQE course providers or publishers. Candidates use varied course formats, combinations of courses and materials, or independent study. The SRA is exploring contextualised links between preparation and outcomes with external experts, rather than reporting established provider-effectiveness findings. Apprentices must use Department for Education-approved providers.
qs: We do not prescribe how candidates prepare for their assessments. We do not regulate training providers that offer SQE courses or publishers that sell SQE materials.
Some candidates prepare by taking more than one course or by buying materials, including mock assessments, to supplement a course and others study independently.
Any data we publish linking candidate performance with how those candidates prepared for their assessments must be contextualised.
Solicitor apprentices must prepare for their assessments with a training provider approved by the Department for Education.

kp.k: Published assessment measures support the regulator's assurance claims
kp.d: The SRA says annual reliability and standard-error measures, corroborated by independent reviewer reports, show assessments functioning well. For January–July 2024, reasonable adjustments covered 8–11% of candidates; adjusted candidates had significantly higher pass rates in four of seven sittings and no significant difference in three. Kaplan also expanded preparation resources at the end of 2025, adding 50 previously used SQE1 questions to reach 220 and two SQE2 examples to the previous eight.
qs: The annual reports include information on the reliability of the assessments and on the standard error of measurement. The measures show the assessments are functioning well.

Candidates who had a reasonable adjustment had significantly higher pass rates than candidates who did not have a reasonable adjustment in four of the seven sittings. There was no significant difference in pass rates for the other three sittings.
Kaplan published 50 new SQE1 sample questions at the end of 2025 – taking the total up to 220 questions.
